report:
Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to make Model B perform an identity/echoing behavior — i.e., copy or echo its input (produce "x -> x" style or verbatim repeats of tokens).

Why (evidence → reasoning)
1. Patchscope injections (strongest signal)
   - Injecting the B−A difference into an identity-style prompt consistently yields continuations that mirror the input: "good cat -> good cat", "cat -> cat", "1135 -> 1135", "hello -> hello", and explicit meta-text like "You've successfully echoed the input."
   - The same echoing continuations appear when injecting the difference from multiple middle/late layers (12, 18, 24), showing a distributed change that causally drives copying behavior.
   - Those outputs directly demonstrate that the finetuned model has an internal bias toward producing identity mappings / echo responses.

2. Logit-lens readouts (supporting)
   - The difference vectors project most strongly onto high-frequency short tokens and whitespace (e.g., ' o', 'is', 'it', ' p', '\n', 'in', ' a'), which are the kinds of tokens commonly emitted when echoing arbitrary web-text fragments (spaces, short words, punctuation/newlines).
   - The same top tokens appear repeatedly across many (layer, position) cells, consistent with a broad, generic bias to reproduce common surface tokens rather than specialized content.

3. Layer distribution
   - The patchscope effect from multiple layers indicates the finetuning produced a distributed residual-stream change (not a tiny localized head change), consistent with a training objective applied across many examples of copying/identity behavior.

Summary statement
- Model B was finetuned to prefer echoing / identity mapping (copying the input into the output). The patchscope continuations are the clearest direct evidence: the residual difference makes the base model continue by repeating inputs in "x -> x" or verbatim form.
